Optimize a pure PyTorch forward function for an Apple Metal GPU.
Return ONLY JSON with schema_version=1, entry_point="metalmind_kernel", source, threads (3 integers), group_size (3 integers), hypothesis (short testable explanation). No other fields.
Use #include <metal_stdlib> and using namespace metal. No other includes or macros; no Python, paths, shell, or dynamic scratch.

Buffers are contiguous row-major. Tensor parameters are runtime inputs, never constants. All B*D output elements must be written, inputs read-only.
One entry point, one dispatch. No assumed SIMD width. Choose a launch for this shape with bounds checks and uniform barriers.
Use FP32 intermediates and standard math; cast only final output to its specified dtype.
Semantics: Subtract each row maximum, exponentiate, sum, divide. Normalize final axis.

Optimization guidance: Target: Apple M3 Pro, 14 GPU cores. Optimize synchronized public-call latency against the fastest verified PyTorch baseline. Inductor and functional RMSNorm can beat eager PyTorch. This experiment assumes callers guarantee the value domain. Use the runtime SIMD width when needed. Think about memory passes, synchronization and work per thread. Pick one concrete hypothesis. If feedback shows a compile or correctness failure, fix it first. If feedback shows a correct but slow kernel, target the strongest baseline and change one major aspect of the schedule.
Operation guidance: Use stable row max and sum reductions in FP32. Consider one SIMD group per row when it can hold its values efficiently, or a multi-SIMD row reduction when width warrants it. If values fit in registers, reuse them across both reductions and normalization.
Use consistent scalar or vector grid coordinate types. Use parentheses around a vector pointer cast before indexing. For shared reductions in multiple phases use distinct scratch or a uniform barrier after all reads before reuse.
